definition: Vivacious means full of lively, charming energy and spirit, especially in social settings.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word vivacious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know vivacious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Everyone's vivacious great-aunt Rosa could turn even a rainy reunion into a party.
Cheerful describes a pleasant, sunny mood; vivacious adds sparkle — an energy that actively charms and animates the people nearby.
Irrepressible is stronger than vivacious: liveliness so overflowing that nothing and no one can dampen it.

Lively means full of energy — a lively debate, a lively puppy, a lively market can all bustle without charming anyone. Vivacious is more particular: the energy is social and winning, sparkle aimed at the people in the room. Lively measures motion; vivacious measures charm.

Spirited means energetic and bold — a spirited defense, a spirited reply, energy with some fight in it. Vivacious keeps the energy but trades the fight for charm: warm, social sparkle that draws people in rather than squaring off with them.

Vivacious means full of lively, charming energy and spirit, especially in social settings.
The new intern, Bea, learned every name on the floor by Wednesday.
She spun her chair around to join conversations, organized a Friday trivia lunch, and somehow made the quarterly budget meeting feel like a game show.
"We hired a spreadsheet analyst," her manager laughed, "and got a vivacious master of ceremonies."
Bea's sparkling, people-focused energy — learning names, launching trivia, making meetings lively — is exactly the charming social liveliness that vivacious describes.
warmly admiring; almost always describes a person

Vivacious praises one person's charming, engaging social sparkle, while its louder cousin boisterous (also in this unit) describes noisy, rowdy exuberance — a whole crowd can be boisterous, but only a sparkling personality is vivacious.

When Marisol arrived from Chile in September, the eleventh grade was a quiet place: lunch tables kept to themselves, and the hallways moved in near silence.
Marisol learned forty names in five days and used all of them, loudly and warmly, in the lunch line.

Teachers described her as vivacious, and the word fit: it was not just that she had energy, but that the energy spilled onto everyone near her — shy kids found themselves talking, and separate tables began pushing together.
By October the cafeteria was twice as loud, and nobody could quite remember how it had been before.
